CHAPTER 21
Amazon RDS Engineering
Managed relational databases, availability, scaling, connectivity, backups, and production
operations
VOLUME 6C | CHAPTER 21
Learning Objectives

Explain what Amazon RDS manages and what remains the customer responsibility.

Select engines, instance classes, storage, Multi-AZ models, and read replicas.

Design private connectivity, credentials, encryption, and connection management.

Operate backups, maintenance, upgrades, monitoring, and failure response.
21.1 Managed relational database responsibility
Amazon Relational Database Service runs supported relational database engines while automating
infrastructure tasks such as provisioning, replacement, patch workflows, backup orchestration, and
monitoring integration. It does not remove the need for schema design, query tuning, transaction
discipline, index management, data classification, access control, capacity planning, and recovery testing. The right mental model is a managed database platform, not a database that operates itself. Engineers still
own application behavior, workload isolation, connection storms, slow queries, lock contention, engine
compatibility, and release safety. Production teams therefore define service standards around engine
versions, parameter groups, option groups where applicable, networking, encryption, observability,
backup retention, and maintenance windows.
21.2 Engine, compute, and storage decisions
RDS supports several relational engines, each with different features, licensing, extension ecosystems,
replication behavior, and operational constraints. Select from application requirements and migration
feasibility rather than personal familiarity.

may fit low-duty development systems but can hide sustained-capacity problems. Storage type, allocated
size, IOPS, throughput, autoscaling limits, and engine-specific behavior must be tested with realistic query
and transaction patterns. A database can be CPU-idle while storage latency or lock contention dominates
user response time.
21.3 High availability and read scaling
A Multi-AZ DB instance deployment maintains a synchronous standby in another Availability Zone and
uses a single endpoint that changes destination during failover. The standby is for high availability and
normally does not serve read traffic. A Multi-AZ DB cluster uses a writer and readable replicas across
three Availability Zones according to supported engine and configuration options.

Read replicas use asynchronous replication and are primarily a read-scaling and migration mechanism. They can also contribute to disaster-recovery designs, but replica lag and unreplicated failures must be
considered. A read replica is not equivalent to a synchronous standby, and promotion is an operational
event that changes recovery and application behavior.
21.4 Connectivity, credentials, and pooling
Place production databases in private subnets with a DB subnet group spanning the Availability Zones
required by the design. Permit inbound traffic only from approved application security groups or network
paths. Public accessibility should be an explicit exception, not a convenience default. Applications should retrieve credentials from a managed secret system and rotate them through a tested
workflow. IAM database authentication is useful for supported engines and access patterns but does not
remove database authorization. RDS Proxy can pool and reuse connections for supported engines, reduce
connection churn, and improve resilience during failover; it must be configured with correct secrets,
network access, TLS, and application behavior.
21.5 Backup, maintenance, and observability
Automated backups provide point-in-time recovery within the configured retention window. Manual
snapshots persist until explicitly removed. Snapshot copy and export patterns support account, Region,
analytics, and governance requirements, but KMS permissions and service support must be validated. A
successful backup job is not proof that the application can be recovered. CloudWatch metrics, database logs, Enhanced Monitoring, Performance Insights or supported
performance tooling, event notifications, and engine-native views should be combined.

CHAPTER 22
Amazon Aurora Engineering
Distributed relational storage, reader fleets, Serverless v2, global databases, and resilient
application design
VOLUME 6C | CHAPTER 22
Learning Objectives

Explain Aurora cluster architecture and endpoint behavior.

Design writer, reader, and custom endpoint usage.

Evaluate provisioned and Serverless v2 capacity.

Use global databases, backups, cloning, and failover appropriately.
22.1 Aurora architecture
Amazon Aurora is compatible with selected MySQL and PostgreSQL ecosystems while using an AWS-
designed distributed storage system. Compute instances attach to a shared cluster volume, separating
much of the storage durability mechanism from individual database instances. This supports rapid replica
creation, managed failover, and storage growth within documented limits. Aurora compatibility does not mean perfect behavioral identity with community engines. Version support,
extensions, parameter differences, SQL modes, replication features, and operational tooling must be
tested. Treat migration as an application and data project, not as a simple endpoint replacement.
22.2 Cluster endpoints and reader scaling
An Aurora cluster exposes a writer endpoint for the current primary instance and a reader endpoint that
distributes connections across available Aurora Replicas. Instance endpoints address a specific member. Custom endpoints can group selected instances for reporting, batch, or tenant isolation. The reader endpoint balances new connections rather than individual SQL statements. Long-lived pools
can remain concentrated on one replica, so application pooling, connection lifetime, and query routing
matter.

can remain concentrated on one replica, so application pooling, connection lifetime, and query routing
matter. Read-after-write requirements must consider replica lag; critical reads may need the writer or an
application consistency mechanism.
22.3 Provisioned and Serverless v2
Provisioned instances provide chosen instance classes and predictable reserved capacity. Aurora
Serverless v2 adjusts database compute capacity within a configured range and can be useful for variable,
multitenant, development, and unpredictable workloads. It still requires minimum/maximum
configuration, monitoring, connection planning, and engine-specific testing. Serverless scaling is not a substitute for query tuning or schema design. A poor query can consume more
capacity and cost while remaining slow. Set capacity ranges from workload evidence, observe scaling and
connection behavior, and confirm feature support in the selected engine version and Region.

22.4 Global Database and multi-Region design
Aurora Global Database connects a primary Region with secondary Regions using dedicated cross-Region
replication. It can provide local reads and regional recovery capabilities, but application architecture must
address write location, DNS or endpoint transition, secrets, networking, promotion procedure, data loss
exposure, and business validation. A global database is not automatically an active-active relational application. Single-writer and conflict
behavior depend on the selected features and design. Run controlled switchovers and failovers, measure
replication lag, and document which operations are safe during degradation.
22.5 Backups, cloning, and operations
Aurora automated backups and snapshots operate at cluster scope. Fast database cloning can create a
copy-on-write cluster for testing, analytics, or release validation without immediately duplicating all
underlying data. Clones still incur compute and diverging-storage cost and require independent security
controls. Monitor database load, waits, connections, replica lag, storage, commit latency, deadlocks, and error logs. Use parameter groups under version control, stage upgrades, and rehearse rollback or blue/green patterns
where supported. Failover priority tiers should reflect instance suitability and business intent.

CHAPTER 23
Amazon DynamoDB and NoSQL Design
Access-pattern modeling, partition keys, indexes, capacity, transactions, streams, and global
tables
VOLUME 6C | CHAPTER 23
Learning Objectives

Model DynamoDB tables from access patterns.

Design partition/sort keys and secondary indexes.

Choose on-demand or provisioned capacity and diagnose throttling.

Use transactions, streams, TTL, backups, and global tables safely.
23.1 NoSQL starts with access patterns
DynamoDB is a managed key-value and document database designed for predictable low-latency access at
scale. Unlike a relational design that often begins with normalized entities, DynamoDB design begins with
the exact requests the application must execute: keys, filters, sort order, cardinality, consistency, latency,
and volume. A table can store several entity types. Composite keys and overloaded indexes can serve multiple access
patterns, but they require disciplined naming, documentation, and validation. A scan is not a replacement
for a missing access pattern. Filters are applied after items are read and therefore may not reduce
consumed capacity as expected.
23.2 Partition and sort keys
The partition key determines the physical distribution of data. High-cardinality, well-distributed keys help
avoid hot partitions. The optional sort key groups related items and supports ordered range queries, prefix
conditions, and composite relationships. Poor key design can throttle one tenant or timestamp while the
rest of the table remains underused. Write sharding, time bucketing, or tenant-key strategies can distribute extreme workloads, but they
increase read and aggregation complexity.

hrottle one tenant or timestamp while the
rest of the table remains underused. Write sharding, time bucketing, or tenant-key strategies can distribute extreme workloads, but they
increase read and aggregation complexity. The goal is not randomization for its own sake; it is predictable
distribution while preserving efficient queries.
23.3 Secondary indexes and consistency
A global secondary index can use different partition and sort keys and is maintained asynchronously. It
has its own capacity and storage behavior. A local secondary index shares the table partition key and must
be defined at table creation. Index projections should include only what the access pattern needs. Base-table reads can use eventually consistent or strongly consistent options where supported. Global
secondary index reads are eventually consistent. Application design must decide which operations require
immediate consistency, conditional writes, version checks, or transaction boundaries.

23.4 Capacity, throttling, and operations
On-demand mode adapts to traffic and simplifies unpredictable workloads. Provisioned mode sets read
and write capacity with optional auto scaling and may be cost-effective for stable demand. Adaptive
capacity helps uneven access but cannot make an unbounded hot key safe. Monitor consumed capacity,
throttled requests, latency, errors, item size, index behavior, and account/table quotas. DynamoDB transactions provide all-or-nothing operations across multiple items and tables within their
documented scope. Conditional expressions support optimistic concurrency and idempotency. Time to
Live removes expired items asynchronously and should not be used as a precise scheduler. Streams
capture item-level changes for event processing, replication patterns, audit workflows, and materialized
views.
23.5 Global tables, backup, and security
Global tables replicate table data across Regions and provide multi-Region, multi-active capabilities
according to the selected consistency mode and service features. Conflict handling, transaction
boundaries, application idempotency, regional dependency readiness, and cost require explicit design. A
multi-Region table does not make every downstream service multi-Region. Point-in-time recovery and on-demand backups protect against logical and operational failures. Use
encryption, private endpoints where appropriate, fine-grained IAM, condition keys, CloudTrail,
contributor insights, and data classification. Avoid granting broad table access when applications require
only specific actions or leading-key patterns.

CHAPTER 24
Amazon ElastiCache and MemoryDB
Caching patterns, Valkey/Redis-compatible systems, Memcached, durability, failover, and
application correctness
VOLUME 6C | CHAPTER 24
Learning Objectives

Differentiate cache and primary in-memory database use cases.

Choose cache-aside, write-through, and session patterns.

Design shards, replicas, endpoints, eviction, and failover.

Operate ElastiCache and MemoryDB securely and observably.
24.1 Cache versus database
A cache stores data that can usually be reconstructed from an authoritative source. Its purpose is to
reduce latency, offload databases, and absorb read bursts. An in-memory database can be the
authoritative store for selected use cases and therefore requires durability, recovery, and stronger
correctness assumptions. Confusing these roles creates data loss or stale-data incidents. Amazon ElastiCache provides managed distributed cache environments using supported engines such as
Valkey, Redis OSS compatibility, or Memcached depending on current service options. Amazon MemoryDB
provides a durable, Multi-AZ, Valkey- and Redis OSS-compatible in-memory database. The selection must
begin with whether data is disposable, reconstructable, and transactionally authoritative.
24.2 Caching patterns and invalidation
Cache-aside loads data on a miss and writes it into the cache. It is simple and common, but the first

25.1 OLTP versus analytical systems
Transactional databases optimize many small concurrent reads and writes with strict transaction

data warehouse separates analytical compute, storage, governance, and workload priorities. Amazon Redshift is a managed data warehouse that uses columnar storage and massively parallel

sort order, distribution strategy, statistics, table maintenance, and query shape influence performance. Modern Redshift automation can manage many choices, but engineers still need to understand data skew,
network redistribution, large joins, and spill behavior. Distribution determines how rows are placed across compute slices. Poor distribution can concentrate
data or force large shuffles. Sort keys influence range elimination and merge behavior.

26.1 Data lake architecture
A data lake stores large volumes of structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data, commonly in
Amazon S3. A usable lake is not a bucket filled with files; it is a governed platform with zones, metadata,
ownership, quality, lineage, retention, access policy, and cost controls. Typical zones include landing/raw, standardized, curated, and consumption. Raw data should remain

columnar formats, and business definitions. Separate accounts, buckets, or prefixes according to security
boundaries and operational ownership.
26.2 Glue Data Catalog and ETL
The AWS Glue Data Catalog stores table and partition metadata used by Athena, EMR, Redshift Spectrum,
and other integrated services. Crawlers can infer schemas, but automatic inference is not governance. Unexpected files can create incorrect types or partitions; production systems should control classifiers,
schema evolution, and catalog change review. AWS Glue ETL can perform serverless data transformation with supported engines and job types. Reliable
pipelines are idempotent, checkpointed, observable, and able to quarantine bad records.

26.3 Athena and file engineering

strongly affected by bytes scanned. Columnar formats such as Parquet or ORC, compression, partition
pruning, projection, compact file sizes, and selective queries reduce scanning. Too many tiny files increase planning and request overhead. Oversized files can reduce parallelism. Partitioning on a high-cardinality or frequently changing field can create catalog and operational
problems. Choose partitions from common predicates and lifecycle boundaries, then verify with query

mature platform can use all three against shared cataloged data while maintaining one security and data-
quality model.

27.1 Streaming system fundamentals
A stream is an ordered sequence of records processed continuously rather than as periodic bulk files. Real-

failure recovery. Most managed streaming paths deliver at least once in some failure scenarios. Consumers must therefore
be idempotent or deduplicate using stable event identifiers and state. Event time, processing time, late
arrivals, and out-of-order records should be explicitly handled.
27.2 Kinesis Data Streams and Firehose
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams provides managed streaming with partitions/shards or supported capacity
modes, retention, multiple consumers, and replay. Partition keys determine ordering and distribution. A
hot partition key can limit throughput even when aggregate capacity appears available. Amazon Data Firehose delivers streaming data to supported destinations with buffering, transformation,
compression, and error delivery. It is appropriate when the goal is managed delivery rather than custom

29.1 Data security layers
